entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer as an evolving ecosystem. It combines computational methods with large-scale profiling of patient cohorts and perturbation experiments in patient-derived tissue models. It builds dynamic models and 'digital twins' of progression from normal tissue to invasive and metastatic disease, using agent-based models and longitudinal cohorts. It applies AI/ML to integrate genomics, transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, glycomics and digital pathology from real-world cohorts and clinical trials. It also runs organoid and organ-on-a-chip perturbation experiments, robotics-enabled high-throughput screening and agentic workflows that pick the next experiments. Disease emphasis is on early cancer evolution (e.g., Barrett's esophagus, ER+ breast cancer) and on biomarkers for early detection and treatment decisions.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, somatic mutation and evolution analysis, ML methods and spatial/single-cell omics; it is less focused on WGS structural variants specifically, and a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines experimental and computational genomics to study how RNA-encoded gene regulatory programs are rewired in human disease, especially cancer. Its cancer work covers RNA regulatory programs in metastasis and liquid-biopsy (cell-free RNA) detection. On the machine-learning side, it works on foundation models of DNA and RNA (Evo 2, Mach-1, CodonFM, BioReason). It also builds virtual-cell models that predict perturbation responses (Tahoe-100M, STATE, GENEVA). Methods include large-scale functional genomics and perturbation screens, together with deep learning.

fit.reason: The lab strongly overlaps with the student's interest in ML methods for genomics and in cancer transcriptomics. It does little on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and only some single-cell perturbation work touches the student's single-cell interest.

entries.name: Van Loo Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops 'molecular archeology of cancer' methods to ask how tumours evolve. It studies subclonal architecture, metastatic spread and the emergence of therapy resistance. The work is mainly computational. It reconstructs tumour evolution from whole-genome sequencing, including copy-number and structural alterations, and from DNA methylation data. It combines large pan-cancer cohorts (the PCAWG analyses in Nature 2020 and Cell 2021) with focused studies of specific tumour types, including gastrointestinal, pancreatic, colorectal and sarcoma cancers. Other published work includes distinguishing neutral evolution from subclonal selection (Nature Genetics 2018) and biallelic mutations across cancer genomes.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with tumour WGS, somatic mutation and structural variant analysis and with computational methods, but little single-cell or spatial omics emphasis, and the lab is in the US, so the student would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine-learning and computational methods to study the molecular mechanisms of cancer development and progression. A core theme is mutational signatures: the SigProfiler tool suite is used to find the mutational footprints of endogenous and exogenous processes in cancer and normal genomes. Related work covers copy-number and structural signatures, APOBEC mutagenesis, and microbial exposures such as colibactin in early-onset colorectal cancer. The lab also uses high-accuracy duplex sequencing of normal tissues to study somatic mutation, aging and cancer predisposition. It also applies deep learning to histopathology slides and works on genomic biomarkers of treatment response.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in somatic mutation and structural-variant analysis, cancer whole-genome sequencing and ML for genomics. Single-cell and spatial omics is the only minor gap, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab characterizes cancer genomes by cataloguing somatic events and the mechanisms behind them. It also interprets cohort-scale data to find driver genes and pathways, risk factors and molecular subtypes. Current interests are tumour heterogeneity and clonal evolution, single-cell analysis of tumours and the microenvironment, drivers of therapy resistance, proteogenomics, and somatic mutations in normal tissues. Methods are computational: large-scale WGS/WES and RNA-seq analysis, bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, spatial analysis, structural-variant analysis and methods development. The lab also builds widely used tools and pipelines, and it works with a large group of staff scientists and software engineers.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with almost all of the student's interests: tumour WGS/RNA-seq, somatic mutation and SV analysis, computational methods, and single-cell and spatial cancer omics. The main caveats are that it is US-based, so a visa may be needed, and that the PhD slots are tied to Harvard programs.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI-driven, mechanistic models of cancer and neurodegenerative disease that turn patient data into more precise diagnosis and treatment. A main thread is mapping subcellular networks and structures, including the Cancer Cell Map Initiative. Another is interpretable ('visible') machine learning, where neural networks are built to follow the hierarchy of cell biology so that predictions in predictive oncology can be explained. Other areas are network biomarkers for cancer and neuropsychiatric disease, epigenetic aging, and bioinformatics software such as Cytoscape and NDEx.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on cancer genomics and computational/ML methods for genomics. It has little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US or UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab uses machine learning to learn evolutionary rules from biological data and then uses those rules to design biology. One theme is learning from nature, for example how the immune system balances short-term protection against long-term adaptability. The aim is to inform more robust therapeutics. A second theme is accelerating evolution with ML-guided approaches. A third is safe biological AI, meaning generative models that let researchers develop countermeasures against harmful biology quickly. The Stanford profiles describe the PI's work as genome language modeling and design across all domains of life. This page does not name the model families.

fit.reason: The lab is strong on ML methods for genomics, which overlaps with the student's computational interests. It does not work on cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutations or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Hsu Lab

Work is mostly genome-engineering and ML tool development, not cancer genomics or patient-data analysis.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetic basis of common diseases using clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. The main topics are neurological, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric traits (migraine, schizophrenia, epilepsy and their comorbidities) plus some cardiovascular traits. Methods are large genome-wide association and sequencing studies, family-based designs, and analysis of population bottlenecks to find low-frequency and rare variants. Palotie also leads FinnGen, a national biobank genomics project, so much of the group's work is large-scale biobank and registry data analysis rather than tumour sequencing.

fit.reason: Overlap is limited to large-scale statistical/computational genomics and rare-variant analysis; the lab does germline population genetics of neuro/psychiatric disease, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS/RNA-seq, somatic structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Villani Lab
entries.focus: The lab maps the human immune system at high resolution, defining immune cell subsets and the rules that govern immune responses in health, inflammation, disease progression and treatment response. Its main methods are single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, systems immunology and computational modelling, applied to datasets of millions of cells from hundreds of patients. It contributes to the Human Cell Atlas Immune Bionetwork, including a pan-disease blood immune cell atlas across about 20 immune-related diseases, and leads the HCA Cell Annotation Platform. A translational program studies immune-related adverse events (colitis, myocarditis, pneumonitis) caused by immune checkpoint inhibitor cancer therapy, using blood and tissue profiling and spatial methods.

fit.reason: It overlaps strongly with the student's single-cell, spatial omics and computational/ML interests and has an immuno-oncology angle, but it centres on immunology rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis.

entries.name: Price Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods to uncover the genetic basis of human disease, along with the population genetics that underpins those methods. One focus is identifying the tissues, cell types and cell subtypes that are critical to disease. For this it combines GWAS data with bulk-tissue or single-cell functional data. A second focus is using molecular traits such as gene expression and protein levels to pinpoint causal disease genes. A third is how negative selection shapes the architecture of common diseases. A fourth is improving fine-mapping and polygenic risk prediction across diverse populations. The work is statistical and computational and centres on germline, population-scale human genetics, not tumour sequencing.

fit.reason: The lab is strong in computational and statistical methods and uses some single-cell data, but it works on germline GWAS and population genetics. It does not cover cancer, tumour WGS/RNA-seq, structural variants or somatic mutation, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells choose fates during development, regeneration and disease. It builds time-resolved single-cell maps of differentiation in zebrafish embryos, human airway epithelium and intestinal organoids, and it uses lineage tracing to link cell state to fate. It develops technologies including the inDrop droplet-barcoding platform and CAGE semi-permeable core-shell capsules, which support multi-step single-cell genomics, live-culture screens and cell-cell interaction mapping. Computational work includes algorithms for lineage-resolved trajectories, noise quantification, and predictive models of tissue behaviour. The lab also does functional genomics in bacteria and comparative immune evolution in Ciona. It does not work on cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in single-cell methods and computational genomics, but it works on developmental fate and technology development. It has no cancer, tumour WGS, structural variant or spatial omics focus, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: O'Donnell-Luria Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses large-scale genomic and transcriptomic data to improve rare disease diagnosis through better rare variant interpretation and discovery of new disease genes. Projects include using gnomAD to estimate rare disease prevalence and to study incomplete penetrance, meaning why some carriers of disease-causing variants never develop symptoms. The lab also uses RNA-seq to resolve variants in unsolved Mendelian cases, interprets noncoding and regulatory variants, and studies unannotated genes using constraint, gene length and age. It contributes to the gnomAD and seqr platforms and to the Rare Genomes Project. The work is germline and Mendelian, not cancer.

fit.reason: The computational genomics, RNA-seq and variant-interpretation methods overlap somewhat with the student's interests, but the lab works on germline Mendelian disease and has no cancer, somatic, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial focus.

entries.focus: The lab develops and applies computational and statistical methods that integrate large-scale human genetics (GWAS) with functional genomics, single-cell data and systems biology. The aim is to identify causal genes and regulatory mechanisms of complex diseases, mainly common eye diseases: age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Projects include splicing QTLs in human retina, integrating single-cell and epigenomic data from eye tissues with GWAS signals, subtyping glaucoma loci, and finding drug-repurposing candidates from expression profiles. Segrè also directs the Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Core in the Ocular Genomics Institute and was part of the GTEx core team at the Broad.

fit.reason: The overlap is in computational and statistical genomics methods and single-cell data integration, but the lab works on germline GWAS for eye disease, not cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptome sequencing, or somatic and structural variants; a US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Neafsey Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies vector-borne disease, mainly malaria. Methods include whole-genome sequencing of parasites and mosquitoes, and low-cost multiplexed PCR amplicon sequencing developed for research and public-health surveillance. Population genomic and bioinformatic methods, especially identity-by-descent relatedness analysis, are used to infer transmission, migration, drug-resistance selection and fitness tradeoffs. The lab also runs molecular surveillance projects (for example in Guyana and Colombia) and distributes its pipelines on the Terra.bio cloud platform.

entries.name: Flannick Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods that use human genetics to understand or treat disease, with a current emphasis on type 2 diabetes. Its main focus is calculating 'genetic support', meaning the likelihood that a given gene plays a role in a disease of interest. The methods are statistical and Bayesian. They model disease genetic architecture, integrate common- and rare-variant association data (including large exome sequencing datasets) with other omic data, and identify shared molecular causes across diseases with similar symptoms. The lab also coordinates the Knowledge Portal Network, which includes the Type 2 Diabetes Knowledge Portal, and serves as the Knowledge Center for the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and statistical genomics methods, but its work is germline human genetics of metabolic disease and data portals, not cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Desai Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies evolutionary dynamics and population genetics, especially when selection is pervasive and shapes genetic variation across a genome. Experimental work uses budding yeast and E. coli, including barcoded lineage tracking, long-term and artificial evolution experiments, and coexistence and diversification. Theory work models allele-frequency trajectories with recombination and background selection, and epistasis in genotype-phenotype maps. Newer directions include machine learning for genotype-phenotype prediction and protein design, and coevolution of pathogens and immune systems such as antibody evolution in germinal centers.

entries.name: Lawrence Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses statistical and computational methods to study somatic DNA alterations in human genomes, including mutations and mutational processes. Its main topics are DNA damage and repair, the link between gene expression and genome replication, and the identification of cancer driver genes. Lawrence developed the MutSig suite, which finds significantly mutated genes against a heterogeneous mutational background in large cancer sequencing cohorts. The lab also analyzes mutational strand asymmetries to separate transcription-coupled from replication-coupled processes, and it has worked on APOBEC3A mutation signatures. It has built the TumorPortal resource, and the DrugMap atlas of cysteine ligandability across 416 cancer cell lines, with Liron Bar-Peled.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation analysis, cancer driver discovery and computational or statistical genomics; less focus on structural variants, single-cell or spatial omics, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on diabetes precision diagnostics and management. It uses genetic data across the spectrum from rare to common variation to find new diabetes genes, subtypes and disease mechanisms. A major theme is clustering type 2 diabetes genetic loci into biological process-specific groups and polygenic scores, including a 2024 Nature Medicine study of more than 1.4 million people across ancestries. The group also leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT study of atypical diabetes, which searches for rare variants. It analyses UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, All of Us and the T2D Knowledge Portal, and it runs a clinical genetics program for monogenic diabetes.

entries.name: Hacohen Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds systems-biology tools and models of immune processes to support personalized immunotherapy. It runs genome-wide genetic screens in primary immune cells, including work that identified STING as a proton channel. It also discovers immune cell types and states for the Human Cell Atlas, including dendritic cell subsets and T cell states, and links cell states to sepsis, lupus nephritis and cancer immunity. In cancer, it works on patient-specific neoantigen vaccines, using machine learning to predict antigens, and on spatially organized immune structures in tumours associated with effective immunotherapy. Several members use single-cell multimodal methods and deep learning.

fit.reason: There is solid overlap with the student's interests in single-cell and spatial omics in cancer and in machine learning for genomics, but the lab is immunology-centred rather than focused on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. It is also in the US, so a visa may be needed.

entries.name: Sabeti Lab
entries.focus: The Sabeti Lab develops genomic and computational tools to detect, track and contain infectious threats such as Ebola, Zika, Lassa, SARS-CoV-2 and malaria. Its work combines pathogen genomics, artificial intelligence, rapid diagnostics and outbreak intelligence. The lab also studies human genetics, building algorithms and molecular tools to find genetic and regulatory variation linked to health and disease, including natural selection in the human genome. It develops countermeasures such as diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines. It also builds outbreak-response capacity through programs such as Sentinel and the African Center of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Disease, mainly in West Africa and the U.S.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works on the mathematical foundations of statistics and machine learning. Current themes are Wasserstein gradient flows and statistical optimal transport, and transformers modelled as interacting particle systems, with self-attention treated as a velocity field. Earlier single-cell work includes Waddington-OT, which was developed with Broad collaborators to reconstruct developmental trajectories in reprogramming from scRNA-seq time courses.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods for large-scale human genetics, using biobank-scale data such as the UK Biobank. Other methods work targets the genetic architecture of complex traits and diseases.

entries.name: Irizarry Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods and open-source software (largely R/Bioconductor) for interpreting large, noisy genomic and molecular datasets. Its work includes single-cell RNA-seq, such as technical variability and GLM-PCA dimensionality reduction. It also covers bulk RNA-seq quantification and normalization (Salmon, Alpine, CQN, DerFinder). DNA methylation work includes BSmooth, Bumphunter and minfi. Cross-cutting themes are normalization, batch-effect correction, and statistical modeling. Older work covers microarray and SNP-chip copy number analysis. The lab also does some public health and data science education work.

fit.reason: The lab's computational methods for single-cell and bulk transcriptomics overlap with the student's methods and single-cell interests, but it is not focused on cancer WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. Roles in the US would also likely need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic changes during cancer evolution shape cancer behavior. Some members add experimental work, for example on DNA-damage repair in pediatric gliomas.

entries.name: Hormoz Lab
entries.focus: The lab asks how biological history shapes future cell fate. It combines experimental, theoretical, engineering and computational work to make those histories observable. Experimental threads include engineering cells to record lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, barcoding cells and reading the barcodes in situ alongside transcriptomes, and long-term time-lapse imaging with mammalian mother machines. The lab also builds human gastruloid and organoid models of early development, including generating blood stem cells from ES cells. Computational and theory threads include differentiable models of development, population genetics and stochastic processes to reconstruct the origins of blood cancers, single-cell RNA-seq for bacteria, and directed viral evolution for gene delivery.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the quantitative control of gene expression in human development and the disease 'tipping points' that can result when expression falls outside a tolerated range. entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational genetics methods to understand the genetic basis of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. The tools are released as open-source software and cloud-scale pipelines. This description of focus comes from my background knowledge and the team page, not from a research page I opened. Applications include spatial proteomics of tissue, such as tumour and tissue-atlas imaging with collaborators like the Angelo lab at Stanford and the Keren lab at the Weizmann Institute. The lab also works on dynamic live-cell imaging and on combining imaging with genomics-style readouts.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interest in machine learning and spatial omics in cancer through its tissue-imaging work. It does little on sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, which are the student's core interests.

entries.name: Winfree Lab
entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Computation and Neural Systems / Bioengineering (molecular programming)
entries.focus: The group studies biomolecular computation, mainly by building computing systems out of DNA. Topics include algorithmic self-assembly (DNA tile and origami systems), enzyme-free DNA strand displacement circuits, and DNA-based molecular robotics. They also work on molecular self-replication and evolution, fault-tolerant molecular computing, and how DNA and RNA fold, interact and are designed at the sequence level. Current members also work on phase separation, pattern formation and morphogenesis in synthetic biology, molecular motors, and oscillating chemical reaction networks. The approach combines theory, computational design and wet-lab experiments.

fit.reason: The lab does DNA nanotechnology and molecular computing, and it has no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant, genomic machine learning or single-cell omics work, so it barely overlaps with the student's interests.

entries.name: Parker Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how organisms interact across species boundaries and how those interactions evolve. Its model group is rove beetles (Staphylinidae). Most species are free-living predators, but hundreds of lineages have become symbionts inside ant colonies. The lab investigates the neural circuits and behaviours behind beetle-ant interactions. It also studies the biosynthetic pathways and specialized cell types that let the beetles chemically communicate with ants and integrate into colonies. Approaches include comparative and evolutionary genomics, developmental genetics and neurobiology.

fit.reason: The lab does insect evolutionary genomics and neurobiology, so it has almost no overlap with cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics in cancer. The only link is general genomics and comparative-genomics skills.

entries.focus: The lab works in synthetic and systems biology, studying the dynamics of gene circuits in cells and developmental systems. entries.name: Guttman Lab
entries.department_hint: Biology and Biological Engineering (experimental plus computational genomics)
entries.focus: The lab studies how long noncoding RNAs organize the nucleus and regulate gene expression. A major model is Xist, which silences the X chromosome. The lab asks how Xist finds its targets through 3D proximity, spreads across the chromosome, and recruits the SHARP/SMRT/HDAC3 complex to shut off RNA Polymerase II. It also studies RNA-seeded nuclear compartments and bodies (nucleoli, speckles, histone locus bodies), imprinting by Kcnq1ot1, and how SARS-CoV-2 proteins bind host RNAs. Methods include SPRITE (mapping 3D RNA–DNA–protein assemblies), RNA–protein interaction profiling, CRISPRi screens, single-cell and high-throughput genomic assays, and microscopy.

fit.reason: The lab is a strong experimental and computational genomics group, and it has some single-cell methods work and a UBC alumnus. But its focus is RNA and nuclear biology and chromatin architecture, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS/transcriptome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutations.

entries.name: Lees Group
entries.focus: The lab studies how pathogenic bacteria evolve to become more pathogenic and transmissible. Its research areas are pangenome evolution, evolution across the whole bacterial domain, and bacterial population genomics. Examples include post-vaccine selection in S. pneumoniae, speciation in Neisseria and Haemophilus, and capsule evolution. It builds evolutionary bioinformatics and modelling software (the bacpop tools on GitHub) that runs in a browser, on a laptop, or on GPUs. It uses machine learning, Bayesian models, dN/dS selection methods, bacterial GWAS and pangenome graphs. It also co-runs the AllTheBacteria resource. This is microbial rather than cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The overlap is limited to computational methods and machine learning for genomics, and to large-scale sequence analysis; the lab works on bacterial evolution and has no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial work. A UK role would also need a visa.

entries.name: Finn Group (Microbiome Informatics)
entries.focus: The group studies whole microbiomes, including the understudied viral and eukaryotic (single-cell) fractions, to understand how microbial communities function and interact. It examines how mobile genetic elements generate genomic diversity, including in opportunistic pathogens and drug-resistant microbes. It adopts long-read sequencing to capture microbial diversity and recover high-quality genomes from low-yield environments. The long-term aim is to understand the role of microbial communities in health and disease, including in under-represented geographic populations, and to support applications such as pathogen surveillance. The team also builds the MGnify resource and maintains the HMMER web server.

entries.name: Keane Group (visiting)
entries.focus: The group does computational comparative genomics, mainly in mouse and other rodents. It studies the structure, function and gene regulation of the most diverse loci in the mouse genome, including strain-specific diversity regions (SSDRs). These regions are enriched for genes involved in immunity, sensory functions, sexual reproduction and behaviour. It produces reference-quality genome assemblies for 16 mouse strains as part of the Mouse Genomes Project. It also sequences other rodents, such as spiny mice (Acomys) and the Algerian mouse, that are relevant to biomedicine and climate. The PI also leads strategic planning for the EGA and EVA data archives and co-leads the GA4GH Large-scale Genomics workstream.

entries.name: Coorens Group
entries.focus: The group develops computational tools for somatic mutation data. These include mutation calling and phylogenetic tree reconstruction, which use somatic mutations as lineage barcodes to trace cell ancestry. They compare mutation rates, mutational processes and cancer-driver genes across normal human tissues, and study how lifestyle, exposures and inflammation shape them. They also build large phylogenies of normal cells to study early embryogenesis and the origins of childhood cancers, by comparing cancer and normal cell lineages. The group is part of the NIH-funded SMaHT Network and the dGTEx Consortium.

entries.focus: The lab studies how gene regulatory networks control the formation of tissues during development. The lab works on normal development and does not study cancer.

entries.name: Manrai Lab
entries.focus: The lab applies machine learning and statistical modeling to medical decision-making. Its topics include AI in medical diagnosis, clinical use of genomic data and blood laboratory biomarkers, inherited heart and kidney disease, and decision-making across diverse populations. It also studies the reproducibility and safety of medical AI, and exposomics. A 2026 Nature Medicine atlas of exposome–phenome associations drew on two decades of NHANES data. fit.reason: The overlap is limited to computational and ML methods in genomics (such as variant pathogenicity work); the lab focuses on clinical AI, population-level inference and exposomics, not cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Patel Group
entries.focus: The group develops computational and bioinformatics methods to analyze large high-throughput datasets, from molecular data to population-level data. It integrates electronic medical records, environmental exposures (the exposome) and inherited genomic variation to dissect inter-individual differences in human phenomes. The lab runs exposome-wide association studies and work on pharmacoexposomics, and it studies multi-omic pathways (proteins, gene regulation, exposures) to health and disease. Other themes are machine learning for personalized and preventive medicine (e.g. diabetes, lung function, brain aging, and some cancer applications) and meta-science on how robust big-data findings are, including 'vibration of effects'.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and machine-learning methods, but its work is population-scale exposomics and epidemiology, not tumour WGS or transcriptome sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutation analysis, or single-cell and spatial cancer omics.

entries.department_hint: Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
entries.focus: The lab does computational biology on the human microbiome, studying how microbial community function relates to human health and disease. It develops bioinformatics and statistical methods and software, including taxonomic and functional profiling of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes and association testing of microbial features with host phenotypes. It applies these methods to large cohorts and consortia, such as the NIH Human Microbiome Project and the HMP2 study of the gut microbiome in IBD. Further work covers microbial strain tracking, metabolomics integration, and nutritional and epidemiological cohort analyses. The focus is on microbial communities, not tumour genomics.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational methods and machine learning for omics, but its work is on microbiome and metagenomics, not cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour WGS or single-cell/spatial cancer omics. The student may also need a US visa.

entries.name: Li Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical algorithms for biological sequence analysis. Its main areas are sequence alignment (bwa, minimap2, miniprot), de novo assembly (miniasm, hifiasm), and variant calling (longcallR, longcallD). It also works on pangenome graphs (minigraph, pangene), full-text indexing (ropebwt3), sequence file formats (SAM, GFA), and population genetics (PSMC). The work is mostly methods and software for long-read and high-throughput sequencing data, and the lab is known for widely used tools such as BWA, minimap2 and samtools.

fit.reason: The lab's long-read alignment, assembly and variant-calling methods (including SV calling) are relevant to structural variants and computational genomics, but it does little cancer-specific, transcriptome, single-cell or spatial work. The one cancer link is a student co-mentored with Matthew Meyerso

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods to characterize the genetic architecture of common disease. The work is mainly statistical genetics on population-scale GWAS and biobank data, not tumour sequencing.

entries.name: Farhat Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses genomics and informatics to improve surveillance, rapid diagnosis and personalized treatment of infections, with a main focus on Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance. Methods include phylogenetic detection of natural selection in the Mtb genome, and studies of pathogen evolution within hosts. They also build machine learning and predictive models linking genotype to antibiotic-resistance phenotype, including neural networks and evolutionary-coupling analyses. Clinical and field work includes EHR-based studies of TB diagnostic delay and partnerships in South Africa and India. Secondary pathogens include other mycobacteria, gram-negative rods, C. difficile and COVID-19.

fit.reason: Strong overlap in computational and ML methods for sequencing data and variant analysis, but the focus is bacterial TB genomics, not cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and the lab is in the US (visa needed).

entries.name: Aryee Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies computational methods to study how spatial organization in tissues relates to normal and disease cell states. It works at three scales. At the tissue scale it uses spatial transcriptomics and chromatin imaging in solid tumours to ask how a cell's neighbours and environment shape its state. At the nuclear scale it studies how changes in nuclear morphology and chromatin packaging in cancer relate to gene activity and disease progression. At the molecular scale it studies regulatory DNA loops, with a current focus on transient promoter interactions. The PI's earlier work, shown in the lab's publication list and in his profile, includes cancer epigenomics, DNA methylation software (minfi) and CRISPR genome-editing off-target detection.

fit.reason: Computational genomics methods, cancer epigenomics and spatial/single-cell omics in tumours overlap with the student's interests, but the lab focuses on chromatin and 3D genome organisation rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis.

entries.name: Avillach Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on translational bioinformatics. It integrates heterogeneous clinical, phenotypic and genomic data from large cohorts and registries. It builds and runs the PIC-SURE platform, which lets researchers securely search and extract arbitrarily large datasets. Projects listed on the DBMI site include the BD2K PIC-SURE Center of Excellence, the Global Rare Diseases Registry, PCORI-funded work on autism-related conditions (ARCH) and Phelan-McDermid Syndrome, and multinational COVID-19 neurological phenotyping. Much of the work is done with Isaac Kohane's group. The emphasis is on data infrastructure, EHR phenotyping and rare disease, not on cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab focuses on clinical and genomic data integration, data platforms and rare disease, so it overlaps only weakly with the student's cancer WGS/transcriptome, structural variant and single-cell/spatial interests. The student would also need a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab uses computational and statistical analysis of large genomic datasets to study the genetic and epigenetic mechanisms behind disease. The lab takes part in large consortia, including SMaHT (somatic mutations in human tissues), 4D Nucleome, the Brain Somatic Mosaicism Network, the Ludwig Center and the International Cancer Genome Consortium. The lab's page does not say which specific methods it uses, but the consortium work centres on somatic mutation, genome structure and large-scale genomic data analysis.

entries.name: Sunyaev Lab
entries.focus: The lab is a computational genomics and human genetics group that studies human population genetic variation. Its topics include the origins of mutations, how allelic variants affect molecular function, evolutionary genetics, and the genetics of complex and Mendelian traits. Its work includes statistical and computational methods for sequencing studies, such as variant-effect prediction and rare-variant and colocalization analyses (for example JLIM). Some work covers somatic mutation, and one student is co-advised with a cancer genomics PI (Eliezer Van Allen). The lab is mostly germline and population-genetic rather than tumour-sequencing or single-cell/spatial focused.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and statistical methods for genomics and somatic mutation analysis, but it focuses on human population and statistical genetics and has little work on tumour WGS/transcriptome, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Keating Lab
entries.focus: The Keating Lab studies how proteins interact with one another, focusing on signaling in eukaryotic cells and its link to human health. It combines computational modeling with experiments to learn how protein sequence determines binding specificity. It also designs peptides and other molecules that selectively disrupt those interactions for research and therapy. Current work centers on Bcl-2 family proteins that regulate apoptosis, using structure-based and machine-learning models to design peptide binders. The lab is extending this to TRAF and EVH1 domains, short linear motifs, and cyclotide yeast display.

fit.reason: The lab works on protein-interaction biophysics and peptide design, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant, or single-cell/spatial omics work; the only overlap is general machine learning methods.

entries.name: Burge Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how gene expression is controlled, combining computational and experimental methods. A central question is how cells recognize introns and splice sites in RNA transcripts, including computational identification of splicing enhancer and silencer motifs that are then tested in living cells. Recent projects include LUC7 proteins and 5′ splice sites in animals and plants, splicing of thousands of random introns, and KATMAP, a tool for inferring splicing factor activity. The group also works on eukaryotic gene finding, microRNA identification and function prediction, and alternative splicing as a regulatory strategy in vertebrates.

entries.name: Page Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how male and female cells, tissues and organs differ at the molecular level, and how those differences affect health and disease. A central theme is the role of the X and Y sex chromosomes in sex-biased conditions such as heart failure, lupus, autism and several cancers. The lab uses natural variation in X and Y copy number in humans to separate effects of the active X from the inactive X, and it finds that the inactive X and its Y counterparts influence gene expression across the genome. It also sequences mammalian sex chromosomes, studies Y-linked gene regulation, and uses mouse models of germ cell development, with relevance to infertility and germ cell cancers.

fit.reason: The lab's genomics and transcriptomics work, plus a bioinformatics team, give some methodological overlap. Its focus is sex-chromosome biology and germ cells rather than tumour WGS, structural variants, somatic mutation or single-cell and spatial cancer omics, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.focus: The group improves force fields for biomolecular simulation, because current force fields can be inaccurate, for example for disordered proteins and protein aggregation. entries.name: Gürsoy Lab
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of genomics and privacy/security. It measures how much private information functional genomics and single-cell data leak, for example a 2024 Cell study quantifying re-identification risk in single-cell data. It also builds tools to protect data at the individual and population level, including privacy-preserving genotype imputation using fully homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based logging of genomic dataset access. A second line of work covers 3D genome organization and chromatin regulatory wiring, and the lab extends privacy methods to EHR and clinical data. Methods are computational: cryptography, statistical and machine-learning methods, and software and pipelines for data sharing.

entries.focus: The lab uses computational biology to analyze large, complex datasets in human health and disease, mainly cancer and neurodegenerative disease. Members also work on immunotherapy-response biomarkers from multimodal data and on single-cell and spatial methods.

entries.name: Alsentzer Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning and natural language processing methods to support clinical decision-making and expand access to high-quality healthcare. A central theme is building trustworthy models that work with limited annotated data and can be deployed safely in clinical workflows. Methods include infusing biomedical knowledge into ML models and reasoning over heterogeneous clinical data such as electronic health records, clinical notes and genomic data. The lab also evaluates model trustworthiness and uses implementation science to integrate models into healthcare systems. Current student projects include longitudinal EHR reasoning linked to patient molecular data and knowledge-grounded language models for rare disease diagnosis.

fit.reason: The lab shares an ML-for-biomedicine angle and has some work linking clinical records to molecular data, but its focus is clinical NLP and EHR. It does not cover cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of bioimaging, spatial proteomics and AI. It maps where proteins sit within human cells and how that organisation affects cell function, and it created the Subcellular Atlas of the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). Current work includes deep-learning and foundation models of immunofluorescence images, protein localisation prediction, 'virtual cell' and digital-twin models, Deep Visual Proteomics, and mass spectrometry for cell-cycle and protein-protein interaction studies. Biological themes include primary cilia, cell migration and metastasis markers, and spatial transcriptomics. The lab also runs citizen-science and crowdsourced machine-learning challenges, such as Project Discovery in EVE Online.

entries.name: Ashley Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on precision medicine. A main thread is interpreting whole-genome sequencing to diagnose rare and inherited disease, especially cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias. The lab combines big-data and network/systems approaches with wet-lab work, using animal models and stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes to test whether key genes are causal. Recent work uses AI: generative protein and DNA models to design gene-delivery vectors and base editors, multimodal clinical models using ECG, echo and MRI, and digital health and exercise-physiology work such as MoTrPAC and elite athletic performance. Cancer is not a focus.

fit.reason: There is some overlap in computational and ML genomics and in whole-genome sequencing analysis, but the lab's work is cardiovascular and rare-disease rather than cancer, structural variants, somatic mutation, or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US visa may be needed.

entries.name: Fries Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops foundation models for healthcare, mainly trained on longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data to model patient trajectories over time. Its themes include self-supervised representation learning and sequence architectures for patient timelines, and multimodal modeling across structured data, clinical notes and imaging. It also works on data-centric ML (data valuation, curation, filtering), post-training and alignment of foundation models, and evaluation and benchmarking of clinical AI with shared datasets. Further topics are capturing tacit clinical knowledge for human-AI teaming and efficient long-context methods. The work is clinical informatics and AI, not genomics or cancer biology.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in machine learning methods, but its work is EHR and clinical foundation models, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics focus.

entries.name: Engreitz Lab
entries.focus: The lab maps the regulatory wiring of the genome to uncover genetic mechanisms of heart development and disease. It aims to link about 2 million candidate regulatory elements to roughly 21,000 genes across thousands of cell types, then uses that map to nominate disease-relevant targets for therapeutics. Methods combine experimental genomics (CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell assays), computational and machine-learning modelling of enhancer-gene interactions, biochemistry, molecular biology and human genetics, including interpretation of noncoding GWAS variants.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and ML genomics and single-cell methods, but it works on non-cancer germline regulatory genetics and heart disease, with no tumour WGS or structural variant focus.

entries.department_hint: Epidemiology & Population Health / Biomedical Data Science
entries.focus: The Witte Lab works on computational and statistical genetics, aiming to find the genetic and molecular mechanisms behind cancer and other complex traits. Current work includes precision screening for prostate cancer (such as genetically adjusted PSA), polygenic risk scores across ancestries, and cross-cancer and multi-phenotype genetics. The work is population-scale genetic epidemiology (GWAS, risk prediction, statistical modelling). It is not tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.focus: The lab treats genomic data as a statistical signal-processing problem and uses statistics, machine learning and deep learning to analyse it. Its main method is SPLASH, a reference-free, alignment-free algorithm that infers sequence variation directly from raw sequencing reads. The lab applies SPLASH to RNA splicing, RNA secondary structure, microbes and viruses, and single-cell data from humans and non-model organisms. It also trains large biological deep-learning models to predict phenotypes such as microbial drug response and single-cell features. Stated interests include splicing, cancer and microbes.

entries.name: Steinmetz Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic variation shapes molecular and cellular traits and disease. It develops genomics technologies to do this, including CRISPR and genome editing, single-cell multi-omics, and spatial genomics. Current projects include modelling inherited heart disease such as dilated cardiomyopathy in stem cells, mice and humans, and mapping enhancer–gene regulatory interactions. The lab also builds synthetic biology systems, including synthetic mitochondria and the Sc2.0 synthetic yeast genome, and runs quantitative genetics CRISPR screens in yeast and human cells. Computational work covers gene-regulation methods and machine learning on perturbation and multi-omic data.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in single-cell/spatial omics and ML for genomics, but its work is functional genetics, genome editing and synthetic biology in yeast and cardiac disease, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variant analysis. A US visa may also be needed.

The lab collaborates with experimental groups and has its own experimental facilities.

entries.name: Linderman Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines statistical machine learning with computational neuroscience. It builds state space models for noisy, high-dimensional neural and behavioral data, including rSLDS, gpSLDS and Keypoint MoSeq. It also works on deep state space models such as S5, and on parallelizing nonlinear sequence models. On the Bayesian statistics side, it develops scalable inference methods: MCMC, variational methods, and latent stochastic differential equations. Applications focus on neuroscience and behavior, not genomics.

fit.reason: The lab's methods (probabilistic ML, Bayesian inference, latent-variable models) could transfer to genomics, but it works on neuroscience and has no cancer genomics, sequencing or variant-analysis focus. The student would also need a US visa.

entries.name: Greenleaf Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops methods and analyses to model the physical genome. One strand is high-throughput biophysics and molecular evolution. It uses ultra-high-throughput bulk and single-molecule assays, in and out of cells, to study how sequence shapes molecular function and interactions. The other strand is DNA accessibility and chromatin structure, starting from the nucleosome. It uses genome-wide assays of open chromatin, nucleosome positions and transcription factor binding in small cell populations. Across both, high-throughput sequencing links sequence, structure, function and physical models. Some current trainees are in cancer biology and computer science, and one is joint with Jesse Engreitz.

fit.reason: The lab's single-cell chromatin and computational methods work overlaps with the student's interest in single-cell omics and ML for genomics. It is mainly regulatory epigenomics and biophysics, not tumour WGS or structural-variant analysis. It would also need a US visa.

It also works on reactive oxygen species control, the systems biology of the unfolded protein response, and cell cycle and cell division. Methods combine high-content microscopy, functional genomic screens, proteomics, mathematical and computational modelling, and bioengineering. The aim is to describe cellular signalling systems quantitatively and find ways to stop cancer cells from changing shape and spreading.

fit.reason: Only a modest overlap: the group uses computational and image-based phenotyping and functional genomics in cancer, but it is not focused on tumour WGS/transcriptome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis.

entries.name: Andrés Group (population/evolutionary genomics), UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The group studies how organisms adapt to their natural environments and how natural selection shapes phenotypically relevant genomic diversity within and between populations. They have mostly worked on humans and other primates, including local adaptation in chimpanzees and humans, and now also work on Drosophila. Methods include population genetics, bioinformatics and genomics applied to modern and ancient genomes, plus functional approaches. Current projects cover balancing selection (including ancestral recombination graph-based inference), experimental evolution to find sexually antagonistic variants, and mito-nuclear co-evolution under introgression.

fit.reason: The lab does evolutionary and population genetics in germline and natural populations. It has no cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic mutation or single-cell work, so overlap with the student's interests is minimal, apart from general computational genomics skills. A UK visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Computational Cancer Biology Group

entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution in cancer. It looks at how mutational processes shape cell plasticity and stress adaptation, and how tumour cells interact with their microenvironment to resist therapy and persist in tissue. It builds statistical, data-integration and machine learning methods that link bulk genomics, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and digital pathology. entries.name: Comparative Somatic Evolutionary Genomics
entries.focus: The group studies how somatic mutations accumulate in normal cells over a lifetime and form clonal expansions that may drive cancer and ageing. They use laser capture microdissection and low-input and duplex sequencing to measure somatic mutation burdens and mutational signatures in normal tissues. The comparative approach spans many species, including non-human primates, other mammals and plants. Three themes run through the work: ageing, cancer resistance across species (Peto's paradox), and using pollutant-linked mutational signatures in sentinel species for environmental monitoring. A Wellcome grant covers somatic mutation and clonal dynamics across about 30 species.

fit.reason: The group overlaps on somatic mutation analysis, mutational signatures and sequencing-based computational methods. It studies normal tissue across species rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Computational Biology of DNA Replication and Repair

The work also asks whether replication errors can be exploited therapeutically in human cancer cells and parasites.

entries.name: Lee-Six Group
entries.focus: The group studies how cells in the body evolve by natural selection and how this can lead to disease, especially cancer. It looks at how genetic changes, the developmental stage at which they arise, and neighbouring cells determine whether mutant cells expand. It is particularly interested in early paediatric diseases, including childhood cancer. Methods combine somatic mutation detection with spatial transcriptomics in human tissue, mathematical models of mutant cell competition, and in vitro tests of the resulting predictions. The long-term aim is treatments that favour healthy cells over those on a path to disease.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation analysis, cancer genomics and spatial omics, but the focus is on normal tissue and paediatric cancer, the group is brand new with no listed members, and a UK role may need a visa.

entries.name: Corander Group
entries.focus: The group works on probabilistic inference, mainly the evolutionary epidemiology of bacterial infectious diseases. It develops statistical and machine-learning methods for bacterial population genomics, including population structure estimation, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and epistasis analysis. It also builds methods for transmission modelling and for genomic surveillance of pathogens, plus software for simulator-based inference. Current projects include BATTALION (E. coli colonization, resistance acquisition and spread) and CARDAMOM (effects of hospital visits and antibiotics on bacteria colonizing infants in a low-resource setting, with Paul Turner at Oxford). Long-term aims include bacterial vaccine discovery.

Topics include sex chromosome evolution (for example X chromosome inheritance in globular springtails), non-Mendelian inheritance such as asexual reproduction and parental bias in transmission, and paternal genome elimination. Work is done largely through large-scale genome comparisons in the Darwin Tree of Life project. The group also builds tools and resources, including smudgeplot for detecting polyploidy and a community database of reproductive metadata.

fit.reason: It is a computational genomics lab, but it works on evolutionary genomics of non-model species, with no cancer, somatic variation, single-cell or spatial focus; the overlap is limited to genome analysis methods and tool development.

entries.name: Blaxter Group
entries.focus: The group studies evolutionary genomics: how genomic novelty arises, and how opportunity and constraint shape present-day diversity. Topics include gene and species phylogenies, horizontal gene transfer and introgression, symbioses between eukaryotes and bacteria and between parasites and hosts, and the evolution of chromosome structure. Much of the work focuses on meiofauna, especially tardigrades, nematodes and other Ecdysozoa, and on the genomics of extremophiles. The group also produces genome assemblies within the Tree of Life Programme and develops software for assembly, validation and analysis.

entries.name: Garnett Group
entries.focus: The group studies how genetic changes in cancer cells affect disease and response to therapy. It runs high-throughput drug sensitivity screens across cancer cell models to find genetic features that predict drug response. It also runs genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to find synthetic-lethal dependencies and new oncology drug targets, for example WRN in microsatellite-unstable tumours. It derives and characterises patient-derived cancer organoids, and uses tumour-immune co-cultures to study how tumour and immune cells interact. It also maintains public resources: the GDSC drug sensitivity database, Project Score CRISPR data and the Cell Model Passports.

entries.name: Stratton Group
entries.focus: The group studies somatic mutations in normal and cancer cells. It uses DNA sequencing to read the changes a genome accumulates over a lifetime, with a focus on the causes of cancer. One main area is large-scale sequencing of normal and cancer genomes to study international differences in mutagenic exposures that may influence cancer incidence. The other is sequencing normal cell genomes (for example by laser-capture microdissection and ultra-accurate NanoSeq) to understand patterns of somatic evolution. Mutational signatures and computational analysis are central, including work on colibactin-producing gut bacteria and colorectal cancer.

entries.name: Lotfollahi Group
entries.focus: The lab uses AI together with experimental techniques to engineer cells and modulate how they respond to disease and perturbations. Its stated vision is a digital version of every human cell across organs, used to engineer resilient cells and design personalised therapies. Biological systems named include large-scale perturbation screens in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, neurulation, T-cell activation and inflammatory gene regulatory networks. The team mixes machine learning, computer science and wet-lab scientists.

entries.focus: The group studies the general principles of how disease-causing bacteria evolve and spread in response to medical treatments, environmental change and the human immune system. It concentrates on multi-strain bacterial populations, and the Imperial profile and job listings name Streptococcus pneumoniae and group B streptococcus. Questions include how antibiotic resistance, virulence and antigen expression arise and move between strains. Methods combine laboratory molecular microbiology, bacterial population genomics and computational modelling. The aim is predictive models of antimicrobial resistance, strain dominance and disease burden, to inform vaccines, diagnostics and public health.

entries.name: Vento-Tormo Group
entries.focus: The group studies the principles of tissue organisation. It combines spatial genomics, single-cell profiling, AI/ML and gene editing to build reference maps of how DNA changes and the environment reshape cellular circuits. A major focus is women's health, including gynaecological and inflammatory conditions, with the endometrium as a model of inflammation resolution and tissue repair. Their iterative approach is to profile patient tissues, predict molecular states with AI/ML, and then perturb in vitro models to establish causality.

fit.reason: The group has strong overlap in single-cell and spatial omics and in computational/ML methods, but its focus is women's health and tissue biology rather than cancer genomics, WGS or structural variants, and a UK role would likely need a visa.

entries.focus: The group studies cancer cell identity and origin, mainly in childhood cancer. It reconstructs the cell of origin of tumours from somatic mutations. entries.name: Google DeepMind
entries.focus: DeepMind's science teams build AI models for biology. AlphaFold predicts protein structures and complexes. AlphaGenome is a sequence-to-function model that predicts how DNA variants affect regulation, including expression, splicing and chromatin. It was published in Nature in January 2026. The AlphaGenome Atlas (September 2026) scores the effects of every possible single-nucleotide change in the human genome. AlphaGenome 2 was announced on 2026-11-11 and is available through an API for non-commercial research. DeepMind also supports cancer-discovery work, including the Azizi team's student researcher placements.

fit.reason: AlphaGenome's variant-effect prediction for non-coding and somatic variants and its ML-for-genomics methods overlap strongly with the student's cancer genomics and structural-variant interests. Access to the programs is competitive and may need a visa.

entries.name: Google Research
entries.focus: The team builds open-source deep-learning tools for genome sequencing data. DeepVariant is a CNN-based germline SNV/indel caller for short and long reads, and DeepTrio extends it to family data. DeepConsensus corrects errors in PacBio long reads, and DeepPolisher polishes assemblies. Together these helped build the human pangenome reference. DeepSomatic (October 2025, Nature Biotechnology) calls somatic SNVs and indels from tumour-normal or tumour-only data on short-read and long-read platforms. It was trained on the CASTLE dataset and tested on pediatric leukemia and glioblastoma samples with UCSC, Children's Mercy and TGen. The group works closely with academic genomics labs such as UCSC (Paten, Miga, Kolmogorov).

fit.reason: DeepSomatic, DeepVariant and long-read tooling closely match the student's interest in tumour WGS, somatic mutation analysis and ML for genomics. entries.name: OpenAI
entries.focus: OpenAI has a dedicated Life Sciences team. In April 2026 it launched GPT-Rosalind, a reasoning model for biology, drug discovery and translational medicine. The model reasons over molecules, proteins, genes, pathways and disease biology, and it uses scientific tools and databases in multi-step workflows. Those workflows include literature review, sequence-to-function interpretation, experimental planning and data analysis. OpenAI reports leading results on the BixBench bioinformatics benchmark and better scores than GPT-5.4 on 6 of 11 LABBench2 tasks. Access goes through Rosalind Workbench and a trusted-access program for qualified Enterprise customers, starting with US organisations. Named partners include Amgen, Moderna, the Allen Institute and Thermo Fisher. A Life Sciences Research plugin for Codex is free on GitHub.

fit.reason: The model covers genomics and bioinformatics analysis, which loosely touches the student's computational genomics interests. However, there is no cancer-genomics research programme, no student-facing life-sciences programme, and the roles are US-based with likely visa barriers.

Anthropic reports that Claude Sonnet 4.5 scored 0.83 on Protocol QA, against a human baseline of 0.79, and says it also improved on BixBench, a bioinformatics evaluation. Anthropic partners with pharma, biotech and academic groups including Sanofi, Novo Nordisk, Genmab, the Broad Institute and Stanford.
